item.title: A question about arbitrary values in USB registry keys
item.description:
USB registry key values decoded: the hex GUIDs under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\USB\Properties aren't arbitrary, they map to documented device property IDs in the Windows SDK header devpkey.h.
- The subkeys under the Properties key store four timestamps as FILETIME blobs, identified by decimal property IDs 100-103 in devpkey.h but displayed as hex 0x64-0x67 in the registry: InstallDate (0x64), FirstInstallDate (0x65), LastArrivalDate (0x66), and LastRemovalDate (0x67). The namespace GUIDs in the key names use commas, not dashes, matching devpkey.h notation.
- Common forensic teaching maps 0x64 to "first install," but 0x64 is actually InstallDate, not FirstInstallDate. FirstInstallDate is 0x65. For USB storage media these two values are nearly always identical, but for other device types they may diverge, so the distinction matters when you need to prove first-ever connection versus most recent install.
- devpkey.h ships with the Windows SDK and is the authoritative source for resolving these property namespaces and IDs. It is also available in WINE-related GitHub repos if you don't have the SDK handy.
- Registry Explorer's USB plugin surfaces both 0x64 and 0x65 side by side, making comparison straightforward during triage.
When documenting USB first-connection time, record both 0x64 and 0x65 and note they match. If they differ, treat 0x65 (FirstInstallDate) as the authoritative first-connection timestamp and note the discrepancy in your report.

item.title: Hackers compromise 14,500 Dahua web cameras in 35-day campaign
item.description:
CameraSwarm: 14,500 Dahua IP cameras compromised in 35 days via brute force, two auth-bypass CVEs, and a cloud-relay attack requiring only serial numbers.
Key findings:
- Three parallel attack methods hit TCP port 37777: brute-force against 12,324 IPs, exploitation of CVE-2021-33044 and CVE-2021-33045 via a tool called p2pwn that drops a persistent backdoor account (username p2pwn / password p2password) on 1,923 cameras, and a cloud-relay attack against 283 NAT-protected cameras using serial numbers plus SDK credentials embedded in Dahua apps. That cloud channel exposed an access path with no authentication on 89.4% of tested serials.
- The p2pwn backdoor account survives password changes and, on most firmware versions, factory resets. Recovery codes derived from the serial number also remain valid until Dahua alters the server-side derivation logic, so account removal alone does not fully remediate.
- Hunt.io recovered 407 MB of operator data from an exposed working directory: source code, shell history, logs, credentials, and captured camera snapshots. Russian 🇷🇺 comments appeared in modified public tools, and scanning prioritized Russian 🇷🇺 and CIS telecom netblocks.
Dahua cameras reachable on port 37777 between June 17 and July 22 should be treated as compromised. Audit for a p2pwn account, apply SA-2021-0130 firmware, and disable P2P if unused. Recovery codes stay live until Dahua acts server-side; credential removal is not enough.

item.title: 41 deceptive download sites show a real link, then send you somewhere else
item.description:
41 typosquat-style sites impersonate Steam titles and Windows apps to bait-and-switch visitors into installing Download Studio via JavaScript click hijacking, bypassing the hover-to-verify safety tip entirely.
Key findings:
- JavaScript cancels the expected navigation on click and routes visitors through an affiliate redirect, making the hover-displayed URL (a genuine Steam or VideoLAN address) meaningless as a safety check. The lures span Counter-Strike, VLC, 7-Zip, Avast, Recuva, and even an impossible GTA VI PC download.
- Download Studio (DS-Setup.exe, SHA-256: 9a3f6e69c12cb814c45862219ecb17e9ab7744877c9da1c49f3ea046437f8fca) is validly signed by Grand Media, TOV. A valid Authenticode signature confirms publisher and integrity but does NOT confirm you got the software you intended, a distinction Microsoft's own docs make explicit.
- History matters: in 2020 Avast documented Download Studio's auto-update mechanism being abused to silently deliver FakeMBAM, a backdoor that dropped crypto miners. The current installer enables auto-updates. No evidence the same attack is active now, but the risk surface is unchanged.
- Network IOCs include C2/redirect infrastructure at r.byteengineering[.]net, apis.downloadstud[.]io, downloadstudio[.]net, and 41 lure domains such as vlcmp[.]ru, csgodownload[.]ru, and gta6-play[.]ru. Full domain list in the report.

Key findings:

- Three access paths ran in parallel: brute-force against 12,300+ IPs, a 2021 Dahua auth-bypass pair that planted a backdoor account named p2pwn on 1,923 cameras (survives password changes and most factory resets), and Dahua's own P2P cloud relay reached via hardcoded SDK credentials shared across every Dahua client ever shipped.
- The offline recovery-code generator is the most dangerous piece: given only a serial number it derives a code that unlocks Dahua's cloud account-recovery flow entirely offline. Removing the backdoor account does not close this. Only Dahua changing the derivation does.
- OEM-rebranded lines built on the same backend are equally exposed: Amcrest, Lorex, Annke, and Swann among them.
Responders: hunt for the p2pwn account, disable P2P where unnecessary, patch the 2021 bypass pair, and rotate all credentials those cameras ever held. The exfiltration bot already grabbed stored passwords.

item.title: AWSHound: An OpenSource AWS OpenGraph Collector
item.description:
AWSHound maps real AWS attack paths across entire Organizations by evaluating IAM policies offline, including SCPs, RCPs, and permissions boundaries, then feeds the result to BloodHound CE for shortest-path analysis.
Key details:
- The core problem: AWS permission evaluation is a four-part question (principal, action, resource, context) assembled from policy stacks owned by different teams. No single tool or console view holds all four. AWSHound runs a full offline policy evaluation before drawing a single edge, so an edge only appears when a principal's effective permissions resolve to Allow after boundaries and SCPs have clipped everything they can.
- The graph model separates traversable edges (36 of 156) from structural ones. Pathfinding follows traversable edges like AWS_CanAssumeRole, AWS_CanUpdateLambdaCode, and AWS_CanCreateAndAssumeAdminRole. Non-traversable edges like AWS_Trusts and AWS_CanDecryptKMSKey stay in the graph for hunting but do not count as movement, because decrypting a key gets you data, not a new identity.
- Conditions on grants are preserved on the edge rather than flattened away, so an sts:ExternalId requirement or a principal tag condition on a trust policy stays visible in the graph properties. Unknowns are evaluated attacker-side: allows that cannot be disproved are kept, denies that cannot be confirmed are dropped, making these candidate paths, not fully materialized ones.

item.title: BOFScale: A CDN-Fronted Tailnet from a BOF-PE
item.description:
BOFScale runs a full Tailscale daemon as an in-process BOF-PE with no driver, no service, and no disk state, routing C2 traffic as standard WebSockets through CloudFront or Fastly.
- Three components work together in-process inside the implant: tailscaled (modified Go daemon compiled as a CGo DLL, async BOF), tailscale (C++ BOF-PE HTTP/1.0 client over a random UUID named pipe), and socksportfwd (async SOCKS5 port forwarder binding 0.0.0.0:1080). State is kept in memory with -state mem:, no WinTun driver is needed via -tun=userspace-networking, and -no-logs-no-support kills telemetry. Child processes were eliminated by replacing ping.exe with direct IcmpSendEcho2 calls and removing wsl.exe and ipconfig.exe invocations.
- The CDN-fronting works because the fork patches Tailscale to speak RFC 6455 WebSockets for both the DERP relay and the TS2021 control channel, which vanilla Tailscale cannot do. Traffic hits CloudFront or Fastly on port 443 as a standard Upgrade: websocket with Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: derp or ts2021 and forwards to a self-hosted Headscale stack. Ephemeral nodes auto-expire after 10 minutes.
- The primary detection signals: Go runtime heap present inside a non-Go host process; a random UUID named pipe with SDDL D:(A;;GA;;;WD); SOCKS5 listener on 0.0.0.0:1080 owned by an unexpected process; and outbound WebSocket upgrades with derp or ts2021 subprotocols from a process that is not tailscaled.exe.

item.title: Ray CVE-2025-62593: Critical Browser-Driven RCE via DNS Rebinding
item.description:
CVE-2025-62593 in Ray is actively exploited and CISA KEV-listed. A DNS rebinding and User-Agent bypass chain lets a malicious webpage submit jobs to a local Ray Dashboard, achieving RCE without credentials.
Key findings:
- CVE-2025-62593 (CVSS 4.0: 9.4 Critical, CVSS 3.1: 8.8 High) affects all Ray PyPI versions before 2.52.0. The Jobs API at /api/jobs/ required no authentication, and the only browser guard checked whether the User-Agent started with "Mozilla". Firefox and Safari allow JavaScript to override that header, so sending "User-Agent: Other" bypasses the check entirely. Chrome blocks the override, making it resilient to this specific path.
- The six-stage chain: victim visits attacker page, DNS rebinding resolves the attacker domain to 127.0.0.1:8265, browser POSTs to /api/jobs/ with a forged User-Agent, Ray accepts the job, and the entrypoint executes with Ray process privileges. Post-exploitation targets cloud credentials, SSH keys, model artifacts, training data, and GPU resources for mining or lateral movement.
- For responders hunting exploitation: look for POST requests to /api/jobs/ with non-Mozilla User-Agent strings, Ray worker processes spawning unexpected shells or interpreters, and DNS telemetry showing short-TTL domains that flip between external IPs and loopback. Check EDR for unusual child processes under Ray and unexplained outbound connections.

item.title: MaaS Campaign Combines ClickFix, ErrTraffic and Cruciferra
item.description:
A MaaS campaign chains ClickFix social engineering, ErrTraffic traffic distribution, and the Cruciferra loader to deliver the Remus infostealer while killing EDR from the kernel using a signed vulnerable driver.
Key findings:
- Compromised WordPress sites carry an obfuscated ErrTraffic JavaScript injection that resolves C2 via the Ethereum blockchain, rotating infrastructure without touching the injected script. Lures impersonate Google reCAPTCHA, Cloudflare Turnstile, or a BSOD prompt and copy a malicious PowerShell command to the clipboard for the victim to run manually (T1204.002, T1059.001).
- PowerShell stages use a legitimate Microsoft-signed binary to sideload the Cruciferra DLL, which then uses process hollowing (T1055.012) to inject the Remus infostealer into ServiceModelReg.exe, a second Microsoft-signed binary.
- Cruciferra abuses the signed vulnerable driver DCRCVDrv.sys to terminate security processes from the Windows kernel (T1562.001). eSentire found 145 hardcoded process names targeted, mostly AV and EDR products. The driver is not on the Microsoft vulnerable driver blocklist or LOLDrivers, so standard blocklist enforcement will not catch it.
- ErrTraffic rents for $380/month; Cruciferra's EDR-kill package for $1,200/month. This campaign illustrates fully outsourced intrusion: delivery, lure, loader, and defense evasion each sourced from separate MaaS providers.

item.title: Fake AI, real malware: Attackers impersonating AI brands
item.description:
AI brand impersonation dominates a year of Sophos MDR casework: fake Claude, ChatGPT, and Copilot sites deliver stealers, backdoors, and a custom Slack-controlled RAT built with an AI coding agent.
- Of 38 confirmed adversarial-AI MDR cases (July 2025-June 2026), 30 were AI software impersonation. The Claude brand was abused in 26 cases. Attack chains lean on InstallFix and ClickFix: victims land on typosquatted sites via malicious ads, copy obfuscated commands, and run them. One fake Claude page triggered an mshta one-liner pulling from download-version.1-9-18[.]com, dropping claude.msixbundle then using irm|iex for in-memory process hollowing. LummaStealer arrived through the same AI-branded infrastructure. A fake Claude site also delivered a DLL-sideloading chain ending in a previously undocumented backdoor Sophos named Beagle (detection: Troj/Beagldr-A).
- A fake Perplexity browser extension distributed via the Chrome Web Store hijacked searches and exfiltrated browsing telemetry through perplexity-ai[.]online in real time. Extensions impersonating multiple AI assistants functioned as infostealers beaconing to C2. Browser extensions deserve the same scrutiny as executables.
- The clearest AI-generated malware case: a financial services org compromised via SQL injection against a legacy PHP app. The attacker deployed web shells, ran Chisel for tunneling, then on MDR-enrolled hosts deployed a custom Rust RAT using Slack as C2.

item.title: Analyzing Stripe Vendors Breach: Confirmed Vendor Exposure and Claims of 20,000 Compromised APIs
item.description:
Threat actor "Satanic" drops 669 Stripe vendors' data and 1,033 live API keys on pwnforums, claims 20,000 total keys compromised with staggered releases planned.
- Initial August 18 dump is 2.37GB of a claimed 33GB haul: vendor directories organized by domain, containing JSON and CSV files with customer PII (names, emails, phone numbers, home addresses, IP addresses at transaction time), invoices, charges, and partial card digits. One single vendor account exposed 22,000+ customers and $5M+ in paid invoices.
- Live "sk_live_" Stripe API keys with charge capabilities confirmed in the leak, granting attackers ability to read customer data, trigger refunds, alter settings, or reroute payments. Internal promotional codes also exposed, enabling immediate revenue drain before vendors detect abuse.
- Attack vector points away from infostealers: no correlated infostealer infections found for affected domains, and victims span entirely different tech stacks. Most likely cause is automated mass-scanning for exposed .env files or debug logs leaking plaintext API keys, or a compromised shared hosting or deployment provider.
Stripe vendors: rotate all "sk_live_" keys immediately, audit .env files and debug logs for public exposure, and check Stripe dashboard logs for unauthorized API calls, refund triggers, or settings changes. Hunt your web-accessible configs before the next batch drops.

item.title: FBI, CISA, HHS update Medusa ransomware advisory, detail RaaS affiliate model, exploited flaws and attack tools
item.description:
FBI, CISA, and HHS update the Medusa RaaS advisory through April 2026, documenting 500+ victims across critical infrastructure and adding granular TTPs, tools, and IOCs responders can act on now.
- Medusa operates a RaaS affiliate model since early 2023, using double extortion. Affiliates pay for access; newer ones have ransom negotiation centrally controlled by developers. Demands are sized to victim revenue and paid in Bitcoin. In one confirmed case, a second actor re-extorted a victim after payment, claiming the first negotiator stole the funds.
- Initial access is opportunistic: unpatched internet-facing systems, not targeted sectors. Medusa leveraged CVE-2026-1731 (BeyondTrust) within 24 hours of its February 2026 disclosure and has exploited flaws up to a week before public disclosure. Interactsh OOB domains oast[.]site, oast[.]pro, and oast[.]fun are used to confirm successful exploitation.
- Post-compromise toolset includes Ligolo-ng, Cloudflared, GSocket, Nezha, MeshAgent, web shells, and legitimate RMM tools (AnyDesk, ConnectWise, SimpleHelp, Splashtop). Credential theft via Mimikatz and Minidump; tools staged inside Windows Defender exclusion folders to evade scanning.
- PowerShell obfuscation uses string fragmentation, in-memory decompression, and command history deletion. Encrypted commands reconstruct payloads at runtime, a reliable EDR blind spot when history logging is not enforced.

item.title: Microsoft Tracks MacSync Stealer by Its Behavior, Not Its Domains
item.description:
MacSync Stealer evades domain blocklists by rotating C2 infrastructure faster than defenders can update them. Microsoft linked 30+ domains to the same campaign by hunting behavior, not addresses.
Key findings:
- Initial access is ClickFix social engineering: victims are tricked into pasting a curl command into macOS Terminal. The payload path follows a consistent /curl/[token] pattern, and native tools (sh, cp, rm, killall) plus osascript calls decode and execute it, blending into ordinary macOS scripting (T1059.004).
- MacSync targets macOS Keychain, browser credentials and cookies, SSH keys, AWS credentials, Kubernetes configs, and Ledger/Trezor wallet data. High-value credential theft, not broad collection.
- Exfiltration uses HTTP PUT requests with distinctive parameters: upload_id, chunk_index, and total_chunks, plus a static API-key header and a macOS User-Agent string. RST Cloud found that static API key shared across four confirmed C2 domains even while build tokens rotated, a durable hunting pivot.
- Post-exfiltration cleanup deletes temporary archives, staging folders, and lock files under /tmp/sync*, reducing on-disk evidence. The behavioral sequence (archive creation, chunked upload, deletion) survives even when artifacts do not.
Hunt for: curl spawning from a Terminal session with --data-binary and API-key headers, osascript chaining rapidly into outbound PUT traffic, and /tmp/sync* archive paths appearing before network egress.

item.title: Balonx Sistema: The Face Behind the PhaaS Affecting Mexican Banking
item.description:
Mexican 🇲🇽 PhaaS platform Balonx Sistema combines real-time WebSocket session hijacking, a Spyroid-based Android RAT, and a fully automated AI vishing module to target 20+ financial institutions at industrial scale.
Key findings:
- Balonx operates as criminal SaaS: weekly subscriptions (3,000-6,000 MXN), Telegram-based affiliate onboarding, Bitso crypto payments, and a SuperAdmin gatekeeping layer. A leaked GitHub repo handed Group-IB visibility into the full affiliate and victim infrastructure. Over 1,100 victims harvested since October 2025, with estimated earnings near $99K USD across just 12 active users.
- The core capability is a persistent WebSocket channel (/ws) enabling live adversary-in-the-middle attacks (T1557, T1111). Operators relay credentials to real bank portals, receive OTP challenges, then push the CODIGO or SMS_COMPRA screen to victims before codes expire, defeating MFA in real time across 14 scripted screen types.
- The Spyroid-based APK (package: sacred.explosion) is delivered via the PROTECCION_BANCARIA screen as a fake bank security app. C2 at 196.251.84[.]11:7771/TCP uses setSoTimeout(0) for a never-expiring socket. Hunt for this package name in mobile MDM telemetry.
- CallFlow (callbalonx[.]info) eliminates human vishing operators entirely: GPT-4o-mini generates dialogue, ElevenLabs synthesizes voice, Whisper transcribes victims in real time, running over FreePBX at 85.31.235[.]109:5160/TCP with 30 concurrent SIP channels.

item.title: CoSnitch: When Your AI Assistant Becomes Its Own Whistleblower
item.description:
CVE-2026-24301 (critical): Microsoft Copilot Personal's CoSnitch chain turns one link click into silent, cross-app data exfiltration with no anomalous signals for defenders to catch.
- CVE-2026-24301 chains three flaws: auto-prompt execution via the undocumented ?autorun=1 URL parameter paired with ?q=, silent OAuth connector exfiltration encoding stolen data as base64 in a URL path fetched by Copilot itself, and indirect prompt injection via web summarization that writes attacker instructions into Copilot's persistent memory store. Patched August 18, 2026. No in-the-wild exploitation confirmed.
- The exfil path is forensically invisible: Copilot issues a standard outbound HTTPS GET to an attacker webhook with the payload in the URL path (e.g., GET /exfil/SGV5LCBNe... to eo8el024afgbal3.m.pipedream[.]net). No anomalous headers, no unusual ports. Security tooling sees routine Copilot URL-fetch behavior.
- Memory poisoning via web summarization survives password changes, session revocation, and device re-enrollment. The only artifact is an entry in Copilot's memory UI, which most users never inspect and no EDR or SIEM currently flags.
- Discovery method is noteworthy: researchers used "meta-hacking," iteratively reframing refusals as follow-up questions until Copilot disclosed an undocumented parameter unprompted. This technique applies to any agentic LLM with a natural language interface.

item.title: Hunting MacSync Stealer infrastructure through behavioral pivots
item.description:
MacSync Stealer rotates through 30+ domains to steal macOS credentials, but its curl command patterns, URI paths, and chunked exfiltration parameters stay constant, giving defenders durable hunt pivots that outlast any single IOC.
- ClickFix social engineering (T1059.004) tricks users into pasting commands into Terminal. curl retrieves payload over /curl/ paths, base64 and gunzip unpack it, then osascript chains AppleScript with sh, cp, rm, mkdir, and killall. Collected targets include Keychain material, browser credentials across Chrome/Brave/Edge/Arc/Vivaldi, SSH keys, AWS creds, Kubernetes configs, Apple Notes, and files with extensions like .pem, .seed, .wallet, and .kdbx from Desktop, Documents, and Downloads.
- Data stages to /tmp/sync* paths, compresses to /tmp/osalogging.zip, splits into chunks, then uploads via curl HTTP PUT with --data-binary, an api-key header, macOS User-Agent, and parameters upload_id, chunk_index, and total_chunks to /gate?buildtxd= URIs (T1030, T1041). Artifacts are deleted post-exfil, but the create-upload-delete sequence is still correlatable.
- Microsoft Defender Experts linked 30+ domains by requiring multiple behavioral traits to align: /curl/, /dynamic?txd=, /gate?buildtxd= URI patterns, curl -k -s --max-time flags, and a static api-key value shared across four confirmed C2 domains even as build tokens rotated per deployment.

item.title: Beware the Ransomware Rescuer: Ransom Busters
item.description:
A ransomware affiliate operating as "Ransom Busters" is contacting victims before attacks go public, posing as a recovery firm while running a secondary extortion scheme across DragonForce, Settra, and Anubis RaaS operations.
Key findings:
- Ransom Busters LTD emails victim domain addresses requesting contact with the CEO or IT leadership, claiming insider access to RaaS admin panels and offering to delete stolen data and provide decryption keys for $20,000 to $60,000. The knowledge of non-public incidents is itself a red flag: legitimate IR firms do not know about attacks before they surface publicly.
- GRIT assesses this is a single ransomware affiliate, not a benevolent third party. Forensic analysis of two separate incidents revealed identical tooling: SoftPerfect Network Scanner for recon, s5cmd for exfiltration to AWS, and the Remotely RMM tool deployed via PowerShell.
- Two hard correlation points across both environments: a backdoor local account created with the password Numlock!123 and the same attacker-controlled hostname DESKTOP-BBETH6K, strongly suggesting one operator rather than a shared affiliate playbook.
- Paying this group guarantees nothing. The affiliate has access to the same stolen dataset as the original RaaS operator, and threat actors routinely retain multiple copies for re-extortion or sale.

item.title: MacSync Stealer: How a Google Search for Claude Led to a macOS Infostealer
item.description:
MacSync Stealer uses Google-sponsored ads and a legitimate claude.ai shared conversation to deliver a six-stage macOS infostealer and RAT, observed hitting a Huntress customer in July 2026.
Key findings:
- Initial access via ClickFix: victim clicks a sponsored Google Ad for "How to install Claude Code on a Mac," lands on a real claude.ai shared-conversation page spoofed as "Apple Support," and pastes a curl one-liner into Terminal. The command fetches a polymorphic 1,442-byte zsh loader, hash-based detection will not work here; hunt on curl spawning Base64-decoded shell content instead.
- Six-stage kill chain: zsh loader, in-memory daemon, server-side AppleScript stealer (never written to disk, logic lives behind an api-key gate), a Mach-O RAT persisting via LaunchAgent plist, a separately signed screen-recording capture agent, and trojanized crypto wallet apps. Stolen data archives to /tmp/osalogging.zip before cleanup.
- The Mach-O RAT connects to 85.206.161[.]241:8443 over WebSocket TLS using its own embedded OpenSSL stack, bypassing macOS trust checks. A fallback C2 domain is XOR-obfuscated with key 0xAA. Credentials are written to .mpwd in the user Home folder for immediate RAT retrieval.
- Stage 6 replaces 60 wallet browser extensions, 21 desktop wallet apps, and 3 hardware wallet companion apps. Trojanized Ledger app serves a fake error page to harvest seed phrases. Unlike passwords, crypto recovery phrases cannot be rotated or revoked.

item.title: TrendAI finds newer US data centers more exposed to OT risks, with 6,300 ICS and BAS devices accessible online
item.description:
6,300 internet-exposed ICS and BAS devices found within 1 km of 1,063 US 🇺🇸 data centers, with newer AI-era facilities showing 13.1% exposure vs 4.9% for pre-2010 sites.
- BACnet (58%) and Fox/Niagara (23%) dominate the exposed protocol mix, meaning HVAC, lighting, access control, and fire systems are the primary attack surface. Honeywell Niagara/Tridium leads vendor exposure at 1,785 devices. Vertiv/Liebert and Schneider Electric presence confirms some devices control the data center's own power and cooling, not just neighboring buildings. CVSSs between 7.5 and 10.0 affect Tridium Niagara and Schneider Electric platforms in the dataset, and three product lines are end-of-life with no patch path.
- The core architectural failure: BAS controllers are bypassing the Purdue Model DMZ entirely, creating direct internet-to-OT pathways from Level 1 through Level 3. Shadow OT is a major driver, facilities teams connecting controllers to business internet without IT involvement, leaving them invisible to security programs.
- NYC Metro holds 1,285 high-confidence exposed devices, Silicon Valley 1,020. 143 multi-protocol gateway devices bridge multiple building systems through a single internet-accessible endpoint, a concentrated pivot risk.
Hunt your perimeter first: run bacnet-info, enip-info, and fox-info Nmap scripts against your IP ranges, then Shodan-query your ASN for BACnet and Niagara banners. Any result with default credentials needs isolation before patching.

item.title: Clop Returns with Custom Implant in Mass-Extortion Campaign
item.description:
Clop returns with a purpose-built PTC Windchill implant exploiting CVE-2026-12569 (CVSS 9.3), an RCE flaw now in CISA KEV, actively exploited to mass-exfiltrate engineering IP and decrypt every credential in the application keystore.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-12569 (CVSS 9.3) gives Clop RCE on PTC Windchill, an industrial PLM platform storing engineering designs and product IP. CISA added it to KEV with a three-day federal patch deadline, consistent with confirmed active exploitation at campaign launch.
- The custom web shell (SHA-256: 321e1fb01eb3462b48ff6ccdef132acc1182e3f7456548439f0d4ead12fd98bf) is a full extortion platform on arrival. A single "S" command triggers the built-in "gs" function, which reads ieStructProperties.txt, decrypts the LDAP manager password, and returns all keystore credentials in plaintext, including AD, VPN, and email service accounts.
- The built-in "fl" function queries Windchill's vault database via the app's own MethodContext and WTConnection classes, writes results to flst.txt, then exfiltrates. A custom Java class loader (Cldr) accepts Base64-encoded ZIP bytecode and runs it in-memory with no files written to disk, enabling ransomware or lateral movement on demand.
- Commands route through the custom HTTP header X-windchill-req, responses are GZIP-compressed. Standard WAFs inspecting only URL paths or request bodies will miss this entirely. TLS inspection and header logging are required for visibility.

item.title: Defenders Arise: Examining 7Zip data extraction with Registry analysis
item.description:
7-Zip leaves Registry breadcrumbs when used to access raw physical disks or sensitive paths, a technique seen in real NTDS.dit theft. Here is where to look and what to hunt.
Key findings:
- The registry key Software\7-Zip\FM holds two high-value values: PanelPath0, which stores the last path open in the file manager, and FolderHistory, which stores a unicode-encoded MRU-style list of folders browsed. A value of \\. in PanelPath0 is a direct indicator the operator accessed the raw physical device view inside 7-Zip.
- FolderHistory and CopyHistory both sit in the 7-Zip hive and are parsed similarly to ArchHistory in the Compression key. New entries are prepended, not appended, so the most recent interaction is at the start of the value data. Entries may only flush to disk on reboot, meaning a live system could hold unsaved history in memory.
- The author confirmed a real case where attackers landed on a domain controller, ran 7-Zip, and exfiltrated NTDS.7z. The \\. path combined with history showing the [SYSTEM] NTFS metadata section or System32\config or the NTDS folder is a strong signal of credential-store access.
- CopyHistory tracks the CopyTo dropdown but does not record what was actually copied out, so it shows intent and target path, not file names.
Takeaway: Add Software\7-Zip\FM to your Registry triage and hunt for \\. in PanelPath0 and any NTDS, config, or sensitive path in FolderHistory.

item.title: Mirage2FA Hijacks Companies’ Microsoft 365 Sessions, with Over 4K Victims in the US
item.description:
Mirage2FA PhaaS bypasses MFA to steal live Microsoft 365 sessions via AiTM, hitting 4,500+ victims across Technology, Manufacturing, and Education since late 2024.
Key findings:
- Attack chain runs entirely in the browser: .htm/.xhtml/.svg stagers decode via XOR key 0xAD + Base64 + eval, retrieve harvesting logic from /[a-z]{3}/xls/[a-z0-9]+.js, then proxy the full M365 login over WebSocket in real time (T1566.001, T1027, T1539, T1557). No binary malware touches disk.
- Session-cookie theft is the dominant outcome: 4,561 of 9,332 recorded compromise events. Password reset alone is insufficient. Full response requires revoking all Entra ID sessions, auditing mail-forwarding rules, and reviewing OAuth grants.
- Infrastructure pivots on the /xls/*.js path and LINX* placeholder tokens (LINXB64EMAIL, LINXCODERSEMAIL). C2 anchor is 185.174.100[.]224 (AS-Colocrossing /24). Known loader domains include user.cheacker[.]store and hvr.volatilesour[.]store.
- 33% of successful logins came from mobile, where limited URL visibility makes inspection harder. Amazon SES was used for high-volume distribution; HR and 401(k) lure themes recur.
Hunt proxy and email gateway logs for GET /???/xls/*.js, outbound WebSocket after JS loader fetch, and Base64-encoded email addresses as DNS subdomain labels. Full IOC list and detection patterns are in the ANY.RUN report.

item.description:

item.title: 600,000 WordPress Sites Affected by Arbitrary File Upload Vulnerability in Forminator Forms WordPress Plugin
item.description:
CVE-2026-15748 (CVSS 9.8 Critical): Unauthenticated arbitrary file upload in Forminator Forms affects 600,000+ WordPress sites, enabling remote code execution via PHP webshell delivery.
- CVE-2026-15748, CVSS 9.8. All Forminator Forms versions up to 1.56.1 are vulnerable. Patch is version 1.56.2, released July 31, 2026. Exploitation requires a published form with both a File Upload field and a Select field present simultaneously.
- The attack chain is a logic flaw, not a simple bypass. An attacker submits a forged Select field value carrying a spoofed Upload record, injecting attacker-controlled field configuration into field_data_array before validation runs. The upload handler then trusts that configuration, including a custom MIME type and extension list.
- The blocklist strips the literal "php" key but not regex-style alternatives. Supplying the pattern ph(p)|text/x-php bypasses exact-key matching in forminator_allowed_mime_types(), while WordPress's extension matcher still resolves ph(p) as .php, letting the file pass validation and land on disk.
- RCE is achieved when the site uses a Custom File Upload Storage root. That directory lacks the .htaccess guard (written only during a specific load context), so a direct HTTP request executes the uploaded PHP webshell. Default upload directories are partially mitigated by .htaccess, but custom roots are not.

item.title: Akira Ransomware Uses Safe Mode to Bypass EDR
item.description:
Akira ransomware affiliate used Safe Mode to kill EDR before encrypting, but the stripped-down memory environment crashed the encryptor. Data was already exfiltrated, so the victim faces extortion regardless.
- Initial access via MFA-less SonicWall VPN at 03:52 UTC on August 4. Two hours of quiet followed before the operator RDP'd to the domain controller, dumped all AD users and group memberships via PowerShell with truncation disabled, archived file shares with WinRAR, and exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled S3 bucket using s5cmd. Encryption came last, meaning failed ransomware does not mean no harm.
- The Safe Mode pivot is new for Akira in Huntress telemetry. The affiliate added AnyDesk to the Safe Mode service registry before rebooting, preserving remote access through the restart (T1562.001). EDR and Defender real-time protection were both down for roughly ten minutes.
- akira.exe launched at 06:34:29 UTC, spawned its child-process burst at 06:36:21, and hit out-of-virtual-memory failures about 13 seconds later. Defender eventually flagged it as Ransom:Win32/Akira.B!ibt but could not quarantine in Safe Mode. Rebooting to normal mode restored Defender, which then removed the file automatically.
Hunt for bcdedit or msconfig.exe activity, Kernel-Boot Event ID 27 with SAFEBOOT option, Kernel-General Event ID 12 with BootMode=2, and third-party services stopping abruptly.

item.title: Three NTFS bugs, one VHD file, and what your logs should already be telling you
item.description:
Three NTFS heap overflows in ntfs.sys, all triggerable via a single malicious VHD file, patched July 2026 across roughly 30 Windows client and server editions. No public PoC confirmed yet, but the forensic window before patching deserves scrutiny.
- CVE-2026-50471 (CVSS 7.8), CVE-2026-50494 (CVSS 7.8), and CVE-2026-58640 (CVSS 7.3) all share the same CWE-122 root cause: ntfs.sys allocates a heap buffer using one size, writes using a mismatched length, corrupting adjacent kernel pool memory. CVE-2026-50494 is the most dangerous operationally as it requires only local low-privilege access with no user interaction to escalate to SYSTEM. The other two need a user to open the file, a trivial social engineering bar given VHD has no "are you sure" prompt on double-click since Windows 8.
- The delivery chain is deliberately low-friction. Windows Explorer auto-mounts a VHD like a ZIP archive. Attackers can deliver it via email, chat, or cloud link with a plausible backup or disk image cover story. APT-C-60 already used VHDX as an attack vector in a documented campaign analyzed by Positive Technologies.
- NTFS itself logs the attack. The USN Journal ($Extend\$UsnJrnl) retains create, rename, and delete events for roughly 20 days even after the VHD is removed. The $LogFile records low-level metadata transactions that can show heap corruption fingerprints even without a system crash.

item.title: Plist Files: Structure, Forensic Value, and How to Analyze Them
item.description:
Plist files are everywhere in Apple investigations: Wi-Fi history, Bluetooth pairings, app state, device identity. Knowing how to read them correctly is not optional for macOS and iOS casework.
Key findings:
- Binary plist (bplist) is the default format since Mac OS X 10.2. It opens with the signature bplist00 and is parsed backward: trailer first (last 32 bytes), then offset table, then root object. The trailer supplies offset integer size, object reference size, object count, root object index, and offset table location. Every other read depends on those values. A parser that hardcodes root object index 0 will silently decode the wrong subtree when the root is elsewhere.
- Dates are stored relative to the Cocoa epoch (January 1, 2001, 00:00:00 UTC), not the Unix epoch. Applying the wrong reference point shifts every timestamp by 31 years. Verify before you report.
- NSKeyedArchiver files embed an object graph using UID references rather than flat key-value pairs. Spotting UID entries in a plist is your signal that you are not looking at a simple settings file. Walking those references by hand is slow and error-prone; the parser must resolve them for you.

item.title: Revisiting JWT Token Forgery Attack on Recent Bounty Target
item.description:
A partner portal accepted unsigned JWTs with alg=none, letting an unauthenticated researcher enumerate the full partner directory, including billing data and contact records, with no valid account or session.
Key findings:
- The API validated that token.partner_id matched the query string id param, but both values came from the forged token itself. The "authorization check" existed and was enforced, yet it compared two attacker-controlled values against each other, making it meaningless (MITRE T1550.001 adjacent abuse of auth tokens).

Records returned account numbers, billing methods, addresses, and company emails with zero rate limiting observed.

item.title: Escalating a Blind Upload to RCE via Path Traversal into Cron and DNS-Restricted Callback Bypass
item.description:
Unauthenticated blind file upload escalated to root RCE via path traversal into /etc/cron.d, bypassing forced UUID/.png renaming entirely. CVSS 3.1 score: 10.0 Critical.
Key findings:
- The endpoint at /app/api/files/upload required zero authentication and passed the uploadPath field directly into a filesystem write with no sanitization, allowing 14-segment traversal (../../../../../../../../../../../../../../etc/cron.d) to escape the upload root and land files anywhere the process could write. Absolute paths, encoded separators, and relative components were all accepted.
- The backend ran as root, confirmed via a blind filesystem oracle: writing to /proc failed (kernel blocks arbitrary directory creation there) while /root and /etc succeeded. This write-only oracle answered yes/no questions about filesystem state by distinguishing directory-creation errors from success responses, enabling host fingerprinting (RHEL/CentOS, crond present, no .dockerenv).
- Cron processed the UUID-named .png as a valid system crontab because it reads directory contents by file content, not extension. A self-removing crontab planted in /etc/cron.d executed as root one cycle later, confirmed by the oracle detecting /tmp/bugbounty-cronproof.
- DNS egress was blocked, but curl --resolve mapped a controlled hostname directly to an attacker IP, bypassing the resolver entirely. The callback returned uid=0(root) gid=0(root) context=system_u:system_r:system_cronjob_t.

item.title: ARM64 stack internals and obfuscation on Apple Silicon
item.description:
ARM64 call-stack spoofing lands on Apple Silicon: MDSec reverse-engineers how to build synthetic frame chains that fool macOS EDR sensors relying on spindump for thread-stack collection.
- A major EDR vendor delegates call-stack collection to /usr/sbin/spindump, macOS's own diagnostic tool. That design choice becomes exploitable: spindump trusts the frame-pointer chain anchored at x29 and return addresses stored at [x29+0x8], walking the linked list without verifying whether frames were built by a real prologue or constructed in memory.
- Synthetic frames work by reversing the unwinder's logic. Pick real executable PCs that have valid __TEXT,__unwind_info entries (compact-unwind mode 0x04000000 FRAME or 0x02000000 FRAMELESS), allocate matching memory at the required x29-relative offsets, then set live x29 and x30 so the unwinder walks the fake chain instead of the real call history.
- On ARM64e Apple Silicon, every saved LR is PAC-signed with key B and the frame's entry SP as discriminator: signedLR = PACIB(rawPC, CFA) where CFA = FP + 0x10. Synthetic frames must replicate this per-frame signing or authentication fails. A trampoline gadget frame, a branch-to-register inside a dylib cache image, bridges the fake chain back to implant code in unbacked memory.
- The DFIR impact: EDR call-stack telemetry on macOS can be fed a fabricated call history (dyld_start, then benign-looking framework symbols, then the target API), hiding the true origin.

item.description:

Key findings:
- The bug lives in nsppe, NetScaler's packet-processing engine, during SAML signature canonicalization. An oversized ds:SignedInfo PrefixList attribute is copied into a fixed-size global buffer without bounds checking, overflowing into the adjacent nsb chunk's header fields at offsets +0x50 (data pointer) and +0x60 (freelist link). SUID is then set on /bin/sh for root escalation from the nobody webserver context.

item.title: Attack of The Extensions
item.description:

item.title: Akira Affiliate Crashes Ransomware After Attempting EDR Evasion
item.description:
Akira-targeted affiliate self-sabotaged encryption by rebooting into Safe Mode, blinding EDR and AV but starving the ransomware of virtual memory before it could detonate.
- Initial access came via credential spraying against a SonicWall SSL VPN with no MFA. The attacker RDP'd to the domain controller, enumerated Active Directory, then moved to an application server and exfiltrated data using s5cmd (a fast S3 transfer tool), completing the double-extortion setup before attempting encryption.

This killed the Huntress agent and disabled Defender real-time protection for the entire Safe Mode window.
- The plan backfired: Safe Mode's constrained virtual memory environment caused akira.exe to hit an "Out of Virtual Memory" error, collapsing the process tree before encryption ran. A host with more RAM or a larger page file may not have been so lucky, and Akira's developers could retool the encryptor to run leaner.
